config.eventName: Spot the Red Flag, Back the Right Company

mithai.name: Mithai Express
mithai.sells: Kaju katli, namkeen, festive gift boxes and a small café menu.
mithai.customers: Families and office buyers; sales spike at Diwali and wedding season. Almost all sales are cash or UPI.
mithai.runs: Founder-led. The Agarwal family owns 68% and runs the business day to day.
mithai.story: Mithai Express has gone from 112 to 185 stores in two years across Gujarat, Maharashtra and Rajasthan, and plans 60 more next year.

sundaram.name: Sundaram Auto Components
sundaram.sells: Brake pads, clutch plates and brake assemblies made at two plants near Hosur.
sundaram.customers: Indian carmakers and two-wheeler makers, on multi-year supply contracts.
sundaram.runs: Second-generation family management with a professional CFO. Pays a dividend every year.
sundaram.story: A steady supplier that rarely makes headlines. It recently won its first order for brake systems designed for electric cars.

voltgrid.name: VoltGrid
voltgrid.tagline: EV charging network in metro cities
voltgrid.sells: Fast-charging sessions at public stations in malls, office parks and highway exits.
voltgrid.customers: Private EV owners, taxi fleets and delivery companies.
voltgrid.runs: Two founders from the power sector, backed by climate-focused venture funds.
voltgrid.story: VoltGrid more than doubled its network to over 1,000 chargers last year and has just closed a ₹300 cr funding round.

brightpath.name: BrightPath EdTech
brightpath.sells: Video courses and mock tests for JEE, NEET and CAT, sold as one-year and multi-year bundles.
brightpath.customers: Students and parents, through the app and through partner tuition centres across tier-2 cities.
brightpath.runs: Founder-CEO and a well-known former coaching-institute teacher. Celebrity brand ambassador signed in FY26.
brightpath.story: BrightPath reported record profits last year and is talking to bankers about a stock market listing.

threadline.name: ThreadLine
threadline.sells: Trend-led women's and men's clothing, with new drops every two weeks.
threadline.customers: 18–30-year-olds, through 80 stores and a fast-growing online shop (22% of sales).
threadline.runs: Founder and creative director with 2 million personal followers. The founder's family owns 64%.
threadline.story: ThreadLine's festive campaigns regularly go viral, and the brand says it is now profitable and growing in every channel.

pinnacle.name: Pinnacle Logistics
pinnacle.sells: Full-truckload freight, warehousing and last-mile delivery for manufacturers and traders.
pinnacle.customers: About 400 business clients across FMCG, electronics and trading companies.
pinnacle.runs: Founder-chairman and a professional MD. Has paid a dividend for eight years.
pinnacle.story: Pinnacle has grown revenue over 20% a year and recently bought a smaller trucking company to expand in the north.

mithai.name: Mithai Express

notes: Store count: 112 at end of FY24, 140 at end of FY25, 185 at end of FY26.
Same-store sales growth (stores open more than 12 months): +6% in FY25, −3% in FY26. Management attributes the decline to 'new stores drawing customers from nearby older outlets'.
Leases: 38 stores opened in FY26 are on 9-year leases with a 5-year lock-in. Minimum lease payments the company cannot avoid over the next five years total ₹410 cr.
Borrowings: ₹105 cr of new term loans taken in FY26 at 9.5% interest, secured on store fit-outs.
Pre-opening costs of ₹14 cr (staff training, launch events) were expensed in FY26, not capitalised.
No shares held by the promoter family are pledged.
statements.auditor: Unmodified opinion. The financial statements give a true and fair view. No emphasis of matter.

key.title: Margins squeezed: profit fell despite 31% sales growth
key.evidence: EBITDA margin fell from 17.0% to 13.5%; net profit fell from ₹40.8 cr to ₹29.1 cr while revenue rose ₹520 cr → ₹680 cr.

key.title: Borrowings doubled and interest cost more than doubled
key.evidence: Borrowings ₹100 cr → ₹205 cr; finance costs ₹6 cr → ₹13 cr.

key.title: Expansion funded with debt, not cash generation
key.evidence: Capex ₹150 cr vs operating cash flow ₹70 cr; gap filled by ₹105 cr of new borrowing.

key.title: Same-store sales turned negative
key.evidence: Note 2: same-store sales −3% in FY26. All growth comes from new stores, which also cannibalise old ones.

key.title: Lease lock-ins make it hard to close weak stores
key.evidence: Note 3: ₹410 cr of unavoidable lease payments over five years on 9-year leases with 5-year lock-ins.

traps: Pre-opening costs expensed (conservative accounting, not a problem)
Tiny receivables (normal for a cash retail business)
Inventory rising in line with store count

intel.title: Peer comparison: sweets and QSR chains
intel.text: Listed sweets and quick-service chains averaged +5% same-store sales growth in FY26, an EBITDA margin of about 17%, and net debt of about 1.2× EBITDA.

outcome.story: Opened just 12 stores as cash got tight. Same-store sales stayed slightly negative and profit was flat. Shares drifted lower, but the business is intact.

sundaram.name: Sundaram Auto Components

pl.label: Exceptional item: gain on sale of land

cf.label: Less: gain on sale of assets

notes: Customer concentration: the largest customer (a leading passenger-car maker) accounted for 41% of FY26 revenue; the top three customers for 72%. Supply contracts with all three run to FY29.
Exceptional item: a ₹28 cr gain on the sale of surplus land at Hosur (sale proceeds ₹35 cr, book value ₹7 cr). This is non-recurring. Excluding it, profit before tax fell from ₹98.9 cr to ₹84.0 cr.
Steel prices rose about 14% in FY26. Contracts allow price increases to be passed to customers with a one-quarter lag.
Receivable days were about 46 in both years.
Borrowings were reduced to ₹35 cr. The dividend was raised to ₹35 cr.
Order book includes a first contract for EV brake systems, starting FY27.
statements.auditor: Unmodified opinion. Key audit matter: revenue recognition on customer price revisions. No exceptions noted.

key.title: FY26 profit boosted by a one-off land sale
key.evidence: ₹28 cr exceptional gain in the P&L. Without it, profit before tax fell from ₹98.9 cr to ₹84 cr.

key.title: Gross margin squeezed by raw material costs
key.evidence: Material costs rose from 62% to 64.5% of revenue; EBITDA margin from 15.0% to 12.5%.

key.title: Heavy customer concentration
key.evidence: Note 1: one customer is 41% of revenue; the top three are 72%.

traps: Falling debt and higher dividend (signs of strength)
Operating cash flow slightly lower (the land gain is removed from it, as it should be)
Receivables growing in line with sales

intel.title: Peer comparison: auto component suppliers
intel.text: Listed brake and clutch suppliers averaged an EBITDA margin of about 13%, receivable days of about 60, and net debt to equity of about 0.3× in FY26.

outcome.story: Steel prices eased and the delayed price increases came through, restoring margins. The EV brake contract started on time. A quiet, solid year.

voltgrid.name: VoltGrid

notes: Network: 410 chargers at end of FY25, 1,050 at end of FY26, across six metros.
Average charger utilisation was 9% in FY25 and 14% in FY26. Management estimates stations break even at about 20% utilisation.
Raised ₹300 cr of equity (Series C) in FY26. Cash at year end: ₹196 cr.
Combined operating and capital spending in FY26 was about ₹233 cr. Management plans to cut capex to about ₹90 cr in FY27.
Borrowings include a ₹40 cr term loan with a covenant requiring minimum cash of ₹60 cr at all times.
Gross margin (revenue less electricity and site costs) improved from 30% to 34% as tariffs were renegotiated.
statements.auditor: Unmodified opinion. The financial statements are prepared on a going-concern basis; the auditor notes the FY26 equity raise in reaching this view.

key.title: Losses widening as the network grows
key.evidence: Net loss grew from ₹60 cr to ₹84 cr.

key.title: Cash runway under a year without new funding
key.evidence: Operating cash outflow ₹53 cr plus capex ₹180 cr; cash ₹196 cr at year end.

key.title: Utilisation still below breakeven
key.evidence: Note 2: utilisation 14% vs an estimated 20% breakeven.

key.title: Minimum-cash covenant could be breached
key.evidence: Note 5: ₹60 cr minimum cash covenant; at the current burn the company would hit it within about 7 months.

traps: Large capex (building chargers is the business model)
Revenue small compared with assets (early-stage network)
Fresh equity raised (honest funding, disclosed clearly)
Receivables rising fast from a tiny base

intel.title: Peer comparison: EV charging operators
intel.text: Global listed charging operators report average utilisation of 12–15%, and most are still loss-making. Those that reached 20%+ utilisation turned EBITDA-positive.

outcome.story: Signed a dedicated-charger deal with a ride-hailing fleet. Utilisation reached 19% and the next funding round was raised at a higher valuation. A risky bet that paid off this time.

brightpath.name: BrightPath EdTech

notes: Revenue recognition: from 1 April 2025, multi-year course bundles are recognised in full when the student activates the account. Previously they were recognised over the subscription period. Under the old policy FY26 revenue would have been about ₹318 cr.

Content development: the company capitalises the cost of producing video lectures, including salaries of faculty and editors. ₹130 cr was capitalised in FY26 (FY25: ₹45 cr), of which ₹74 cr was employee cost.
From FY26 the useful life of capitalised content was extended from 3 years to 10 years. This reduced the amortisation charge by about ₹21 cr.

Trade receivables (₹120 cr) are mainly from channel partners (tuition centres that sell courses on BrightPath's behalf). ₹48 cr is due from EduReach Partners LLP, in which the spouse of a director is a partner. ₹52 cr has been outstanding for more than 180 days.
Raised ₹80 cr by issuing shares to an investment fund, and ₹60 cr of new borrowings.
Advertising includes ₹38 cr for a celebrity ambassador contract.
statements.auditor: Unmodified opinion, with an Emphasis of Matter drawing attention to Note 1 (change in revenue recognition) and Note 3 (change in the useful life of content). Key audit matter: recoverability of receivables from channel partners.

key.title: Receivables grew far faster than revenue
key.evidence: Receivables ₹45 cr → ₹120 cr (+167%) while revenue grew 58%. Receivable days about 115.

key.title: Capitalised content ballooning: costs moved off the P&L
key.evidence: Capitalised content asset ₹75 cr → ₹193 cr.

key.title: Deferred revenue fell while revenue jumped
key.evidence: Deferred revenue line fell ₹55 cr → ₹48 cr despite 58% sales growth: revenue is being pulled forward.

key.title: Record profit but negative operating cash flow
key.evidence: Net profit ₹57 cr vs operating cash flow −₹7 cr; spending funded by new debt and equity.

key.title: Revenue recognition changed to upfront
key.evidence: Note 1: multi-year bundles now booked on activation; old policy gives ~₹318 cr revenue.

key.title: Amortisation life stretched from 3 to 10 years
key.evidence: Note 3: cut amortisation by ~₹21 cr, flattering profit.

key.title: Related-party and overdue receivables
key.evidence: Note 4: ₹48 cr due from a firm linked to a director's spouse; ₹52 cr over 180 days.

key.title: Auditor emphasis of matter
key.evidence: Auditor flags the policy changes and receivable recoverability.

traps: High advertising spend (normal for consumer edtech)

intel.title: Peer comparison: listed edtech
intel.text: Listed edtech peers capitalise 10–15% of their content spend and amortise it over 3 years. Their receivable days average about 25, and deferred revenue usually grows with sales.

outcome.story: The listing was shelved. The new CFO restated revenue to the old policy, channel partners defaulted on ₹40 cr, and the auditor qualified the next accounts.

threadline.name: ThreadLine

pl.label: Purchases of stock-in-trade (net of inventory change)

bs.label: Advances to suppliers & other current assets

notes: 80 stores; online sales were 22% of FY26 revenue.
Inventory of ₹230 cr includes ₹74 cr of stock older than 12 months from past collections. No provision for obsolescence has been made, as management expects to sell it through outlet channels.

Related party: 38% of FY26 purchases (about ₹173 cr) were from Kesar Textiles Pvt Ltd, owned by the promoter's brother. Management states these were at arm's length. Advances to suppliers include ₹25 cr paid to Kesar Textiles.
Promoter shares pledged with lenders: 62% of the promoter holding (FY25: 15%).
Borrowings rose by ₹110 cr, mainly working-capital loans at 12.5%.
Gross margin improved to 50% from 48%, which management attributes to 'better sourcing'.
statements.auditor: Unmodified opinion. Key audit matter: valuation of inventory, including the ageing of stock and management's estimate of net realisable value.

key.title: Inventory nearly doubled while sales rose 15%
key.evidence: Inventory ₹120 cr → ₹230 cr; about 240 days of stock vs about 140 last year.

key.title: Borrowings and interest cost jumped
key.evidence: Borrowings ₹70 cr → ₹180 cr; finance costs ₹8 cr → ₹16 cr.

key.title: Advances and other current assets jumped
key.evidence: Advances to suppliers & other current assets ₹18 cr → ₹45 cr.

key.title: Gross margin rose while unsold stock piled up
key.evidence: Gross margin 48% → 50% in a discount-heavy industry, while inventory doubled: old stock is not being written down.

key.title: Profit up but operating cash flow negative
key.evidence: Net profit ₹46 cr vs operating cash flow −₹54 cr, driven by the inventory build-up.

key.title: ₹74 cr of old stock with no provision
key.evidence: Note 2: stock older than 12 months, no obsolescence provision.

key.title: Large purchases from the promoter's brother
key.evidence: Note 3: 38% of purchases from Kesar Textiles, plus a ₹25 cr advance to it.

key.title: Promoter pledge jumped to 62%
key.evidence: Note 4: pledged share of promoter holding up from 15% to 62%.

traps: Large influencer marketing spend (normal for the brand)

intel.title: Peer comparison: fast fashion retail
intel.text: Indian fast-fashion peers run inventory of 90–110 days and gross margins of 45–48%. Most write down stock older than 9 months.

outcome.story: Took a ₹60 cr inventory write-down. Lenders sold some of the pledged promoter shares after the price fell, pushing it lower still. Kesar Textiles came under a lender review.

pinnacle.name: Pinnacle Logistics

notes: Revenue from Orion Trade Links Pvt Ltd was ₹378 cr (28% of FY26 revenue; FY25: 12%). Orion and Pinnacle share a common director.
Of trade receivables of ₹420 cr, ₹265 cr is due from Orion Trade Links. ₹150 cr has been outstanding for more than 180 days. No expected-credit-loss provision has been made.
Unbilled revenue (services rendered but not yet invoiced) was ₹62 cr (FY25: ₹18 cr).

Acquisition: bought 100% of SwiftHaul Carriers Pvt Ltd for ₹110 cr from entities controlled by a relative of the promoter. Net assets acquired ₹20 cr; goodwill ₹90 cr. SwiftHaul's FY26 revenue was ₹28 cr.
Contingent liability: a disputed GST demand of ₹85 cr, not provided for.
Change of auditor: the previous auditor resigned in February 2026, stating that information it requested on certain related-party balances was not provided. A new auditor was appointed in March 2026.
Dividend of ₹25 cr paid in FY26.
statements.auditor: Qualified opinion. The auditor was unable to obtain sufficient evidence on the recoverability of ₹265 cr receivable from a related party, and could not determine whether any adjustment to these accounts is needed.

key.title: Receivables up 83% vs revenue up 23%
key.evidence: Receivables ₹230 cr → ₹420 cr; receivable days about 76 → 114.

key.title: Unbilled revenue and other current assets surged
key.evidence: Unbilled revenue & other current assets ₹50 cr → ₹95 cr.

key.title: Goodwill jumped after an acquisition
key.evidence: Goodwill ₹20 cr → ₹110 cr.

key.title: Record profit but negative operating cash flow
key.evidence: Net profit ₹98 cr vs operating cash flow −₹82 cr.

key.title: Borrowing to pay dividends
key.evidence: Borrowings ₹240 cr → ₹500 cr while paying a ₹25 cr dividend with negative operating cash flow.

key.title: 28% of revenue from a related party
key.evidence: Note 1: Orion Trade Links shares a director; ₹265 cr of receivables are from Orion.

key.title: Overpaid for a related-party acquisition
key.evidence: Note 4: ₹110 cr for a firm with ₹20 cr net assets and ₹28 cr revenue, bought from the promoter's relative.

key.title: Previous auditor resigned over missing information
key.evidence: Note 6.

key.title: Qualified audit opinion
key.evidence: Auditor could not verify the ₹265 cr related-party receivable.

key.title: Unprovided ₹85 cr tax demand
key.evidence: Note 5: contingent GST demand of ₹85 cr.

traps: Fleet capex (normal for a logistics company)

intel.title: Peer comparison: freight and warehousing
intel.text: Listed logistics peers run receivable days of 60–70 and convert about 70% of EBITDA into operating cash flow. Related-party revenue above 10% is rare.

outcome.story: Orion Trade Links defaulted. ₹230 cr of receivables were written off, a forensic audit was ordered, and the company's credit rating was cut to junk.

items.text: ThreadLine crosses 5 million Instagram followers after a viral festive campaign.
Pinnacle Logistics named 'Warehousing Company of the Year' by a trade magazine.
Sundaram's largest customer announces a 6% production cut for one quarter due to a chip shortage.
items.note: Sounds alarming, but short-lived and Sundaram's contracts run to FY29.

items.text: BrightPath's CFO resigns with immediate effect, citing personal reasons.
VoltGrid in final talks with a ride-hailing fleet operator for 400 dedicated chargers.
Tax officials search the offices of Orion Trade Links, a large customer of Pinnacle Logistics.
Mithai Express says it will pause new store openings to 'focus on existing stores'.

items.note: Small input-cost relief; does not fix the inventory problem.

items.text: Lenders ask ThreadLine's promoter for extra collateral after a fall in the share price.
